name: Micah
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah (about 740–690 BC), before and after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC; Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12. Among the ancient manuscripts, as reported in the published editions, portions of Micah survive in the Qumran scrolls of the Twelve (4QXII-a, 4QXII-f, 4QXII-g), in a commentary from Qumran (1QpMic), in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll (Mur 88), and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. Versification: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14, and English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this translation follows the English numbering.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Micah{a} of Moresheth{b} in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah,{c} which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

For look: Yahweh is coming out from his place;
he will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.

The mountains will melt beneath him,
and the valleys split open,
like wax in front of the fire,
like water poured down a slope.

All this is for Jacob’s rebellion,
for the sins of the house of Israel.
What is Jacob’s rebellion?
Is it not Samaria?
And what are Judah’s high places?{d}
Are they not Jerusalem?

“So I will make Samaria a rubble heap in the open country,
a place for planting vines;
I will tumble her stones down into the valley
and lay bare her foundations.

For the inhabitants of Maroth{k} writhe, waiting for good,
because disaster has come down from Yahweh
to the gate of Jerusalem.

Harness the chariot to the steeds,
inhabitants of Lachish!{l}
She was the beginning of sin for Daughter Zion,
for in you were found the rebellions of Israel.

Make yourself bald, shear your hair,
for the children you delight in;
widen your baldness like the vulture’s,
since they are carried away from you as captives.

notes.text: The name is a short form of Micaiah, “Who is like Yahweh?” Compare 7:18.
Moresheth-gath (1:14), a town in the Shephelah about 22 miles (35 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem.
Jotham reigned about 750–735 BC, Ahaz about 735–715 BC, and Hezekiah about 715–686 BC.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Targum read “what is the sin of the house of Judah?”
Hebrew “hire,” the wage of a prostitute, a figure for the wealth gained through idolatrous worship.
An echo of David’s lament in 2 Samuel 1:20. In verses 10–15 each town’s name is the basis for a play on words, most of which cannot be carried into English.
“House of dust.”
“Beautiful town.”
Sounds like the Hebrew for “come out.”
The meaning of the last line is uncertain.
Sounds like the Hebrew for “bitterness.”
Lachish sounds like the Hebrew rekesh, “steeds.” It was Judah’s second city, besieged and taken by the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC.
Or “a dowry,” as for a bride leaving home.
Achzib sounds like ʾakzab, “deceptive,” a stream that dries up.
Hebrew yoresh, “one who takes possession,” a play on Mareshah.
The cave where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1); Israel’s leaders will be fugitives again.

verses.text:
Woe to those who plan iniquity
and work out evil upon their beds!
When morning dawns they carry it out,
because it is in the power of their hand.

They covet fields and seize them,
and houses, and take them away;
they defraud a man and his household,
a man and his inheritance.

So this is what Yahweh says:
“See, I am devising evil against this clan,
and you will not slip your necks out from under it,
nor stride along with heads held high;
it will be a time of calamity.

In that day they will take up a taunt against you
and wail a bitter lament, saying,
‘We are utterly ruined;
he exchanges the portion of my people.
How he takes it away from me!
To traitors he divides our fields.’

Therefore you will have no one to cast the measuring line by lot{a}
in the assembly of Yahweh.

Should this be said, house of Jacob?
“Is the Spirit of Yahweh impatient?
Are these his deeds?”
Do not my words do good
to the one who walks uprightly?

But lately my people have risen up as an enemy.
You strip the robe off the cloak
from those who pass by trustingly,
like men returning from war.

The women of my people you drive out
from their pleasant houses;
from their young children you take away
my splendor forever.

Get up and go,
for this is no place of rest;
because of uncleanness it will destroy,
with a grievous destruction.

If a man walking in wind and falsehood should lie, saying,
“I will preach to you of wine and beer,”
he would be the preacher for this people!

The one who breaks open the way goes up ahead of them;
they burst out, they go through the gate
and leave by it.
Their king goes on in front of them,
Yahweh at their head.”

notes.text: That is, no share when the land is divided again.
Hebrew naṭaph, “drip,” used of prophetic speech, as in Amos 7:16. The Hebrew of verses 6–11 is difficult in places.
Hebrew Bozrah, here probably “an enclosure,” though Bozrah was also a city of Edom famous for its sheep.

verses.text:
And I said:
Hear now, heads of Jacob
and rulers of the house of Israel!
Is it not for you to know justice?—

who eat the flesh of my people,
strip off their skin,
break their bones,
and chop them up like meat for the pot,
like flesh in a cauldron.

Then they will cry to Yahweh,
but he will not answer them;
he will hide his face from them at that time,
because they have made their deeds evil.

This is what Yahweh says concerning the prophets
who lead my people astray,
who, when they have something to chew,
cry “Peace!”
but declare holy war against anyone
who puts nothing in their mouths:

But as for me, I am filled with power,
with the Spirit of Yahweh,
with justice and with might,
to declare to Jacob his rebellion
and to Israel his sin.

Hear this, heads of the house of Jacob
and rulers of the house of Israel,
who abhor justice
and twist all that is straight,

who build Zion with bloodshed
and Jerusalem with wrong.

Her heads give judgment for a bribe,
her priests teach for a fee,
her prophets divine for money;
yet they lean on Yahweh and say,
“Is not Yahweh in our midst?
No disaster will come upon us.”

So on your account
Zion will be plowed like a field,
Jerusalem made a mound of rubble,
and the mountain of the house a forest height.{c}

notes.text: Hebrew “from them.”
Hebrew “mustache,” a gesture of mourning or shame (Leviticus 13:45).
This verse is quoted in Jeremiah 26:18, about a century later, where the elders recall that Hezekiah heeded it and sought Yahweh’s favor.

verses.text:
In the days to come{a}
the mountain of Yahweh’s house
shall stand firm as the highest of the mountains,
lifted up above the hills,
and peoples shall stream to it.

Many nations shall come and say,
“Come, let us climb to the mountain of Yahweh,
to the house of Jacob’s God,
so he may instruct us in his ways
and we may walk in his paths.”
For instruction{b} shall go out from Zion,
and the word of Yahweh from Jerusalem.

Each shall sit beneath his own vine and his own fig tree,
with no one to make them afraid,
for the mouth of Yahweh of Armies{c} has spoken.

For all the peoples walk,
each in the name of its god,
but we will walk in the name of Yahweh our God
forever and ever.

“In that day,” declares Yahweh,
“I will gather the lame
and assemble the scattered,
those whom I have afflicted.

The lame I will make a remnant,
and the outcast a mighty nation;
and Yahweh will reign over them on Mount Zion
from now on and forever.

And you, tower of the flock,{d}
hill{e} of Daughter Zion,
to you it will come—
the former dominion will return,
the kingdom of Daughter Jerusalem.”

Now why do you cry aloud?
Is there no king in you?
Has your counselor perished,
that pangs have gripped you like a woman in labor?

Now many nations
are gathered against you,
saying, “Let her be defiled,
and let our eyes gaze on Zion.”

But they do not know
the thoughts of Yahweh;
they do not grasp his purpose,
how he has bundled them like sheaves for the threshing floor.

notes.text: Verses 1–3 are nearly identical to Isaiah 2:2–4; Micah and Isaiah were contemporaries.
Hebrew torah.
Hebrew YHWH tsebaʾot, traditionally “the Lord of hosts”: Yahweh as commander of the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Hebrew Migdal-eder, perhaps a watchtower over Jerusalem; compare Genesis 35:21.
Hebrew Ophel, the fortified hill south of the temple mount.
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “push.”
Hebrew “devote to destruction” (ḥerem), here meaning to dedicate the plunder wholly to God.

verses.text:
Therefore he will give them up until the time
when she who is in labor has given birth;
then the rest of his brothers will return
to the people of Israel.

He will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of Yahweh,
in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God.
And they will dwell secure, for now he will be great
to the ends of the earth.

They will shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword,
the land of Nimrod{f} at its gates;{g}
he will deliver us from Assyria
when it comes into our land
and treads within our borders.

Then the remnant of Jacob will be
among many peoples
like dew from Yahweh,
like showers on the grass,
which wait for no one
and do not linger for mortals.

And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations,
in the midst of many peoples,
like a lion among the animals of the woods,
like a young lion among the sheepfolds,
which, when it goes through, treads down and mauls,
and none can deliver.

Let your hand be lifted over your foes,
and may all your enemies be cut off!

I will cut off the cities of your land
and tear down all your strongholds;

I will cut off the sorceries in your hand,
and soothsayers you will have no more;

I will cut off your carved images
and your sacred pillars from among you,
and never again will you bow
before what your own hands have made;

I will uproot your Asherah poles{h} from among you
and destroy your cities.{i}

And in anger and wrath I will take vengeance
on the nations that have not obeyed.”

notes.text: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14. The meaning of the first line is uncertain; perhaps “gash yourself, daughter of raiders.”

English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this verse is Hebrew 5:1. Ephrathah is the clan district around Bethlehem, the hometown of David (Ruth 4:11; 1 Samuel 17:12), about 6 miles (9 kilometers) south of Jerusalem. Matthew 2:6 quotes this verse, in a free form, as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem; compare John 7:42.
Or “from days of eternity.” The phrase may refer to the ancient line of David or, as Christian interpreters have understood it, to the ruler’s origin before time.
Or “This one will be peace,” or “This will be our peace.”
“Seven… eight” is a Hebrew idiom for “more than enough.”
The legendary founder of Mesopotamian cities (Genesis 10:8–12).
So the Hebrew; with a slight change, “with the drawn sword.”
Wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah.
Or, with a slight change, “your idols.”

verses.text:
Hear now what Yahweh is saying:
“Rise, plead your case before the mountains,
and let the hills hear your voice.”

“My people, what have I done to you?
How have I worn you out? Answer me!

For I brought you up from the land of Egypt
and ransomed you from the house of slavery;
I sent before you Moses,
Aaron, and Miriam.

With what shall I come before Yahweh
and bow down to God on high?
Shall I come before him with burnt offerings,
with calves a year old?

Is Yahweh delighted by rams in their thousands,
by oil flowing in ten thousand streams?
Shall I give my firstborn for my rebellion,
the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

Can I forget{j} the treasures gained by wickedness
in the house of the wicked,
and the short measure{k} that is accursed?

Shall I acquit the one with crooked scales,
with a bag of false weights?

So I in turn have begun to strike you,{l}
to lay you waste because of your sins.

You will eat but not be satisfied,
and hunger{m} will remain within you;
you will put things aside but not save them,
and what you save I will give to the sword.

notes.text: Hebrew rib, a formal legal complaint; the mountains and the foundations of the earth are summoned as witnesses (compare Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2).
See Numbers 22–24.
Shittim was Israel’s last camp east of the Jordan (Numbers 25:1; Joshua 3:1); Gilgal its first camp west of it (Joshua 4:19).
Or “saving acts.”
Hebrew ʾadam, “human being.”
Hebrew ḥesed, loyal and steadfast love.
Or “carefully, attentively.”
So the Septuagint, reading the Hebrew with different vowels; the Masoretic Text reads “sees.”
The meaning of the Hebrew of this line is uncertain; perhaps “Hear, tribe and assembly of the city.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Hebrew “the lean ephah.” The ephah was a dry measure of about two-thirds of a bushel (22 liters); merchants used undersized measures to cheat buyers.
Or, following the Septuagint, “I have made you sick by striking you.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.
Omri and his son Ahab, kings of Israel in the ninth century BC, were remembered for Baal worship and injustice (1 Kings 16–21).
Hebrew “her.”

verses.text:
Woe is me! For I have become
like one at the gathering of summer fruit,
like the gleaning after the grape harvest:
no cluster to eat,
no early fig that I crave.

Their hands are skilled at evil;
the official asks for gifts,
the judge for a bribe,
and the great man speaks out what his greed desires—
so they weave it together.

The best of them is like a briar,
the most upright worse than a thorn hedge.
The day of your watchmen,{a} your punishment, has come;
now will be their confusion.

Rejoice not over me, you my foe!
I have fallen, yet I will get up;
I sit in the dark,
yet Yahweh is a light to me.

I will bear Yahweh’s anger,
because I have sinned against him,
until he takes up my case
and brings about justice for me.
He will lead me out to the light;
I will see his saving righteousness.

Then my enemy will see,
and shame will cover her,
she who said to me,
“Where is Yahweh your God?”
My eyes will look upon her;
now she will be trampled
like mud in the streets.

A day for building your walls!
On that day the boundary will be far extended.{c}

Yet the land will lie waste
on account of those who dwell in it,
the outcome of their doings.

Shepherd your people with your staff,
the flock that is your inheritance,
who live alone in a forest
in the midst of a fruitful land;{f}
let them graze in Bashan and Gilead
as in days long ago.

As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt,
I will show them{g} marvelous things.

Who is a God like you,{h}
pardoning iniquity
and passing over the rebellion
of the remnant of his inheritance?
He does not cling to his wrath for all time,
for faithful love is his delight.

He will again have compassion on us;
he will tread our iniquities underfoot.
You will cast all our{i} sins
into the depths of the sea.

You will show faithfulness to Jacob,
steadfast love to Abraham,
as you swore to our ancestors
from the days of old.

notes.text: That is, the day the prophets warned of.
Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 10:35–36; compare Luke 12:53.
Or “the decree will be far removed.” The meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew matsor, “Egypt” or “fortress,” a play on words.
The Euphrates.
Hebrew Carmel, “garden land,” perhaps also the mountain of that name.
Hebrew “him.”
A play on Micah’s name, “Who is like Yahweh?” (1:1).
So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate; Hebrew “their.”
